guide.summary: GitHub OAuth apps are self-serve. You register the app under your account, and any user can authorize it with no app review. The friction comes later: organizations with OAuth app access restrictions need an owner to approve your app before it can touch private org resources. OAuth apps also get lower rate limits than GitHub Apps, which GitHub recommends instead. Composio has managed auth for GitHub, so start there and bring your own app when your users need to see your app's name on the consent screen or you hit rate limits.

reasons_to_bring_own: The application name you register is shown to users during authorization, so your own app is the only way to put your brand on the consent screen.
OAuth apps have lower rate limits that do not scale, and rate limit increases are granted per OAuth app, so heavy usage may need its own app.
Organizations with OAuth app access restrictions approve specific apps, so org owners may prefer to approve an app that carries your name.
build_or_borrow.verdict: Use Composio managed auth; you do not need your own app yet because GitHub needs no review for users to authorize, so switching to your own app later costs only a few minutes of registration.

prerequisites.text: A GitHub account you can log in to. The app registration pages sit behind a login wall.
An application name, which users see during authorization, and a homepage URL. The description is optional.
An authorization callback URL where users are sent after they authorize.
A safe place to store the client secret before you generate it, because it is shown only once.

oauth.token_lifetime: With expiring tokens enabled, access tokens last 8 hours and refresh tokens expire after 6 months without use. Authorization codes expire after 10 minutes.
redirect_uri_rules: Register one authorization callback URL on the registration form. Users are redirected there after authorizing.

blockers.text: Organizations with OAuth app access restrictions require owner approval. Until an owner approves, your app sees only that organization's public resources.
blockers.workaround: Tell users to ask their org owner to approve the app. Detect missing private org data and show that instruction in your UI.

blockers.text: Users who have not verified their email address cannot authorize an OAuth app.
blockers.workaround: Catch the failure and tell the user to verify their GitHub email, then retry.

blockers.text: Flagged or restricted GitHub accounts cannot authorize third-party apps at all. The cause is not email verification or org approval.
blockers.workaround: No workaround from your side. Surface a clear error so the user can take it up with GitHub.

app_specific_gotchas.text: The client secret is shown only once at generation. If you lose it you must generate a new one.

At most ten tokens are issued per user/application/scope combination, and only ten tokens can be created per hour. Agents that re-run the flow often can quietly invalidate older tokens or hit the cap.
The repo scope grants full access to public, internal and private repositories. There is no narrower private-repo option in the claims, and scopes never grant more than the user already has.
GitHub publishes no OAuth or OpenID discovery document. Hardcode the endpoints.
PKCE works only with S256. The plain method is rejected. The device flow is off until you enable it in the app settings.

agent_can: Write the authorization code flow integration against the known authorize and token endpoints, including S256 PKCE.
Draft the application name, homepage URL and description for the registration form.
List the callback URL to register.
Write error handling for unverified email, restricted accounts and org approval cases.
Lay out the trade-off between an OAuth app and a GitHub App.
human_must: Log in to GitHub and register the OAuth app.
Generate the client secret and store it securely, since it is shown only once.
Enable the device flow in app settings if you need it.
Decide whether to use an OAuth app or a GitHub App, which GitHub recommends.
Request rate limit increases for the app if needed.

scope_tiers.gate: No GitHub app review. The user consents on the authorize screen. For organizations with OAuth app access restrictions, an org owner must approve the app, otherwise only that org's public resources are reachable. Scopes never grant more than the user already has.

paths.verdict: Trivial. Register the app under your own account and authorize it yourself. No review, no waiting. Use a verified email on the test account.

paths.verdict: Easy. GitHub has no app review: any user with a verified, unflagged account can authorize your app the day you register it. The real cliffs are org owner approval for restricted orgs (timing is up to each org, not documented) and OAuth app rate limits that GitHub itself says do not scale. Decide OAuth app vs GitHub App before you build.

steps.title: Decide: OAuth App or GitHub App
steps.detail_md: GitHub recommends GitHub Apps over OAuth apps. OAuth apps have lower rate limits that do not scale, and increases are granted per OAuth app. This guide covers the OAuth app path. The agent can lay out the trade-off, but the developer makes the call because it shapes how every user connects. If you would rather not run your own app, Composio lists managed auth for its GitHub toolkit. That route is not covered by the claims here.

steps.title: Draft the registration form values
steps.detail_md:
Prepare the following values:
- **Application name** (required). Users see it on the consent screen.
- **Homepage URL** (required).
- **Description** (optional).
- **Authorization callback URL** (required). This is where users land after authorizing, so list the exact production callback your backend will serve.

No discovery document exists on github.com, so these values cannot be fetched automatically.

steps.title: Log in and register the OAuth app
steps.detail_md: Sign in to GitHub. The developer settings page sits behind a login wall. Then open github.com/settings/applications/new, or go to Settings > Developer settings > OAuth Apps > New OAuth App. Paste the drafted values and submit. The client ID is issued on registration.

steps.title: Generate and store the client secret
steps.detail_md: On the app settings page, generate a client secret. It is shown only once. Copy it straight into your secret store before leaving the page.

steps.title: Enable device flow (only if your agent runs headless or in a CLI)
steps.detail_md: Device flow is off until you enable it in the app's settings. Skip this step if you only use the browser redirect flow.

steps.title: Pick the minimum scopes
steps.detail_md: Scopes only limit what a token can do. They never grant more than the user already has. Avoid `repo` unless you truly need it, because it gives full access to public, internal and private repositories. The agent drafts the list and the developer approves it. The full scope catalog is not covered by the claims here.

steps.title: Implement the authorization code flow
steps.detail_md:
1. Redirect the user to GET https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize. If you use PKCE, use S256, because plain is not supported. The implicit grant is not supported.
2. Exchange the code at POST https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token with client_id, client_secret and code.
3. Do the exchange immediately, because the code expires after 10 minutes.

steps.title: Implement token storage and refresh
steps.detail_md: With expiring tokens enabled, access tokens last 8 hours and refresh tokens expire after 6 months without use. Refresh proactively. At most ten tokens are issued per user/application/scope combination, and only ten tokens can be created per hour, so reuse stored tokens instead of re-authorizing on every session. How to toggle expiring tokens is not documented in these claims.

steps.title: Implement device flow (if enabled in step 5)
steps.detail_md:
1. Start at POST https://github.com/login/device/code.
2. Show the user the code and https://github.com/login/device.
3. The device code expires after 15 minutes by default.
4. Code submissions are capped at 50 per hour per application, so poll politely.

steps.title: Test end to end with your own account
steps.detail_md: Run the full connect flow while logged in. Your account's email must be verified or authorization fails. The authorize URL sends signed-out users to the GitHub login page first, so test that path too.

steps.title: Ship to users and document the failure cases
steps.detail_md:
No app review is required. Any user can authorize the app as soon as it is live, so there is no provider wait. Write user-facing help for these blockers:
- **Organizations with OAuth app access restrictions** need owner approval. Until then, the app sees only that organization's public resources.
- **Unverified email** blocks authorization.
- **Flagged or restricted accounts** cannot authorize third-party apps at all.

drivers: org owner approval for restricted organizations

belief_diff.topic: Does letting arbitrary users connect require provider review or verification?
belief_diff.prior_belief: No, GitHub OAuth apps let any GitHub user authorize them immediately without any review or verification by GitHub.
belief_diff.finding: Claims confirm GitHub does not require app review before arbitrary users authorize, but a user must verify their email address first, and flagged or restricted accounts cannot authorize third-party apps.

belief_diff.prior_belief: There is no approval process for GitHub OAuth apps, so the wait time is zero, and registration takes effect instantly.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say no app review is required, but organizations with OAuth app access restrictions require owner approval before the app can access their private resources, and claims do not address registration timing.

belief_diff.topic: Limits while the app is unapproved
belief_diff.prior_belief: There is no unapproved state, and OAuth apps have no user cap; the only practical limit is GitHub's global API rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour per authenticated user.
belief_diff.finding: Claims state a token cap of ten tokens per user/application/scope combination and a rate of ten tokens created per hour, which contradicts the 'no user cap' belief; claims also say OAuth apps have lower rate limits that do not scale, and do not mention the 5,000 figure. Unapproved orgs get only public resource access.

belief_diff.prior_belief: No, registering and using a GitHub OAuth app is free with no fees or paid plan required.
belief_diff.finding: The claims do not address pricing or fees.

belief_diff.topic: Key prerequisites (domain, privacy policy, video, business verification)
belief_diff.prior_belief: Only an application name, homepage URL, and authorization callback URL are required, with no domain verification, privacy policy, demo video, or business verification needed.
belief_diff.finding: Claims confirm the form requires an application name, homepage URL, and authorization callback URL, and that the description is optional; claims do not address domain verification, privacy policy, video, or business verification either way.

belief_diff.prior_belief: An OAuth app has one authorization callback URL, and the redirect_uri sent in requests must match it or be a subdirectory/same host and port with a path under it, while GitHub Apps allow multiple callback URLs.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say the registration form requires an authorization callback URL, but do not address whether only one is allowed, the subdirectory matching rules, or multiple callback URLs for GitHub Apps.
